goal: Teach one concrete operator lesson with specific examples and conviction.
expected_facts: Early-stage startups can sell to CIOs if the value is differentiated and the risk to the buyer is contained.
CIO trust matters more than polish on day one; founders need credibility, responsiveness, and a plan to close gaps.
Founders should not try to bypass enterprise constraints entirely; they should frame the relationship as a pragmatic pilot with clear ROI.

Explains why trust and buyer risk matter in enterprise sales.
Includes at least one concrete example, scenario, or metric.

gold_reference: A strong answer argues that even a tiny SaaS team can sell to a CIO, but only when the founder understands the buyer's social contract: do not create career risk, be honest about what is missing, show fast ROI, and build trust directly. The piece should emphasize that CIOs can back startups when the upside is meaningful and the initial blast radius is small.

answer:
So I had this interesting conversation recently with a very senior IT leader at one of SaaStr Fund’s portfolio companies that sells into enterprises, especially larger ones (think $100m+ ACV).  They are doing well now, but when they started off, they didn’t really understand how to sell up.  To the CIO level, the VP level, the business process owners.
A few years back, we did a deep dive on “how to sell to CIOs” with the CIO of Workday,
a great session you can watch here:
But my experience is most founders aren’t sure how to do it.   They want their product to be used by everyone across an enterprise, ideally starting with the CEO and going all the way down through sales reps and engineers.  But most CEOs don’t know enough to buy software themselves, no matter how cool it is.  And most CIOs will want nothing to do with anyone who hasn’t worked in tech for decades, unless they’ve been truly vetted as part of their own network.  That leaves VPs of Sales and Engineering … often the #2 and #3 folks in any org.  Not exactly what many start-ups want to try to sell to.
The thing is, if you can get past them — they’ll almost always buy more than just your core app.  More features, more seats, more modules, etc.  So there is real revenue there, even with just an 8-person team.  It’s hard to close big deals without a brand behind you.  Or so it seems.
Here was our experience at Adobe Sign / EchoSign:
We closed some pretty big deals early on ourselves, but once we got past a few $500k-$1m deals, we needed a partner with us.  We added a local reseller, and then later, a channel manager, and then eventually, a global channel director.  Later still, we hired a Global Channel Head from Salesforce to build out a full channel strategy.

Well, maybe you can't sell to their budget owners per se. But you can definitely sell to their point guys. Monday IPO’d
and is now worth $15B (!)
has gone multi-product
and added Marketing and IT as its third core vertical (in addition to Sales & Service) — although we’re still seeing the earliest signs here
has become very enterprise
, with almost half their customers paying $50k+ annually
is going global fast,
with over 100 countries using its product

$500M ARR, Growing 93%
110% NRR overall, And 125% From Its Largest Accounts
126% Revenue Growth Year Ago When It Was At $240,000,000 in ARR
A Stunning 86% Growth Rate in New Customers This Year
What We Can All Learn:

#1. 120% NRR from 10-Seat Deals = Plenty Of Room For Expansion
.  As you can see below, Monday gets even better NRR once your deal goes into double digits.  So if you haven’t really gone all-in on adding more products after $10k deals close … well, maybe start ASAP.
#2.  85% NRR from Smaller Customers Still Drives Them To $250m ARR and Beyond
.  Even small accounts grow quickly.  You don’t need perfect NRR at first.  Just enough to scale quickly.
#3.  40% of Customers Use More Than One Product, Up From 28% a Year Ago.  Push Harder Here
.  Another example of how important multiple products often are.  Especially when they aren’t truly natural extensions like Slack + HypeChat.
#4.  60% of Customers Are Outside North America, and That’s Where They Are Really Accelerating
.  This is a reminder to go where your competition isn’t strong.
